newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss hunt Solar Temple members after Canada deaths.
newsitem.headline: Swiss hunt Solar Temple members after Canada deaths.

text.p: Swiss authorities vowed to crack down on suicide cults on Monday as police began a search for members of the Solar Temple sect after five members including two Swiss men died in Canada in an apparent suicide pact.

The five, including two French women and a Canadian woman, died in Canada's Quebec province on Saturday in a blazing house owned by a member of the doomsday cult, which believes death by ritualized suicide leads to rebirth in a place called "Sirius."

Swiss police said they were monitoring known members of the sun-worshipping cult in Switzerland, most of them well-off professionals who are taught the world will end in fire and that to reach the afterworld they must die violently by burning.
French police said similar measures were taken in France.

The Order of the Solar Temple received worldwide attention in October 1994 when 53 of its members died in a mixture of murder and suicide in two Swiss villages in the cantons of Fribourg and Valais and a ski resort in Quebec.

A year later, in December 1995, 16 cult members including several children died in a remote French Alpine forest clearing in a macabre ritual in which most of them were drugged and had plastic bags pulled over their heads before they were shot.
Police said the deaths on Saturday in Saint Casimir, a village 37 miles (60 km) southwest of Quebec City, appeared to be a suicide pact.

Those who died were the Swiss owner of the house, Didier Queze, 39, his French wife, Chantale Goupillot, 39, her 63-year-old French mother, Suzanne Druau, Swiss Bruno Klauss, 49, and Pauline Rioux, 54, a Quebec Canadian.
Swiss police have come under fire for not taking action against the surviving cult members. They claim they were blocked by the constitutionally-guaranteed freedom to worship.
Gerard Ramseyer, the top justice and police official in the canton of Geneva, warned of a risk of similar deaths in Switzerland and called for measures to monitor the cult.
The cult was known to place great importance on astronomical events, and the latest deaths could have been timed to coincide with the spring equinox, which occurred on Friday.
But Ramseyer said the end of the millenium could also turn out to be a disastrous time for the cult's followers.
"The risk of similar deaths here exists. The same thing could happen here," he told Reuters. "These are mentally fragile people. The end of the millenium will be a difficult time."
Ramseyer said the cult had some 20 known followers in the international city of Geneva and perhaps hundreds in Switzerland out of an estimated membership of some 2,000 in the world.
He said police had great difficulty in tracking them down. "This is a very secretive sect. We first have to find them."
Ramseyer wants new measures including an information campaign at schools about sects and the right to remove a child from its parents' custody if they indoctrinate the minor in a sect.
He said officials in Geneva were working on new measures to keep a tab on members of the Solar Temple and other cults.
Fribourg cantonal police said they had contacted two-thirds of the people in Switzerland associated with the cult and that there was no evidence of a similar disaster in Switzerland.
In Geneva, police spokesman Jacques Valery said none of the known cult members in the region appeared to have been missing.
Swiss classical music conductor Michel Tabachnik, who has acknowledged having cult members as friends but insists he broke all ties in 1994, called the Canada deaths massacres.
The Swiss news agency ATS quoted Tabachnik as saying that he himself had been a cult victim. "I violently condemn these massacres," he said.

Tabachnik's first wife died in the cult's initial group killings in the Swiss village of Cheiry in October 1994. His name has appeared in cult documents and witnesses have told investigators he played an important role in the sect.
